lessons.title: Identifying Common Vegetable Pests
lessons.body: Start by walking your plot every morning at 7am. Look under leaves, inside flowers, and at the growing tips. Common pests in Africa include aphids (small green or black clusters on new shoots), whiteflies (tiny white flies that rise when you shake a plant), thrips (slender, jumpy insects that cause silvery streaks), and caterpillars (holes in leaves and dark droppings). Also watch for larger pests: cutworms cut seedlings at soil level, snails and slugs leave slimy trails and ragged holes, and nematodes cause stunted plants with swollen roots. Learn to tell damage types: chewing mouthparts (caterpillars, beetles) leave holes; sucking mouthparts (aphids, whiteflies) cause yellowing, curling, and sticky honeydew. Use a hand lens (10x) to see tiny pests. Scout at least twice a week. For every pest, note the crop, date, and number per plant. For example, treat aphids if you find more than 10 per leaf. Keep a notebook. Early detection saves money. If you see ants running up and down stems, they are farming aphidsâcontrol ants first. For soil pests, dig 15cm deep in 5 spots per bed and sift soil to find grubs or nematode cysts. A simple yellow sticky trap (yellow plastic coated with grease) catches whiteflies and aphids; hang 10 per hectare. Pheromone traps for diamondback moth (available in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa) help monitor. Remember: not every insect is a pest. Ladybirds eat aphids; bees pollinate. Only spray when pest numbers cross thresholds. For beginners, the rule is: if you see 5 or more pest insects per plant on average, act. Otherwise, wait and watch.

lessons.title: Implementing Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
lessons.body: IPM means using many methods together, not just chemicals. Start with prevention: plant resistant varieties (e.g., tomato 'Tengeru' for bacterial wilt), rotate crops, and keep the field clean. Next, monitor with weekly scouting and sticky traps. Then decide action based on thresholds. For aphids on kale, threshold is 10 aphids per leaf. For caterpillars on cabbage, 2 larvae per plant. If below threshold, do nothing. If above, start with physical methods: handpick caterpillars, wash aphids off with a strong jet of water, or use row covers (fine netting) to keep whiteflies out. Next, use biologicals: release ladybirds or lacewings, or spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) for caterpillars. Only if those fail, use botanical sprays (neem, garlic, chilli). Chemical pesticides are last resortâchoose soft ones like soap or neem oil, and rotate modes of action. Never spray when bees are active (early morning or evening is better). Always follow label rates; overuse kills beneficial insects and causes resistance. Keep records: date, pest, action, result. IPM saves money: a 2019 study in Kenya showed IPM farmers spent 40% less on pesticides and had 20% higher yields. Train your workers to recognise pests and beneficials. Set up a 'pest corner' with flowering plants (sunflower, marigold) to attract predators. For soil pests, solarise soil by covering with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks during hot season. Combine methods: rotate, then monitor, then act. IPM is not organic-only; it's smart farming.

lessons.title: Using Biological Controls and Beneficial Insects
lessons.body: Beneficial insects eat pests for free. The big four in Africa are ladybirds (eat aphids, whiteflies), lacewings (eat aphids, thrips, caterpillars), hoverflies (larvae eat aphids), and parasitic wasps (lay eggs inside caterpillars and aphids). You can buy them from suppliers like Koppert or Real IPM (Kenya, South Africa). But you can also attract them. Plant strips of sunflower, marigold, coriander, and dill around your vegetable beds. These provide nectar and pollen for adult beneficials. Avoid broad-spectrum pesticidesâthey kill good bugs. For a quick boost, release 10,000 ladybirds per hectare when aphids appear. For caterpillars, spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) at 1g per litre of water; it only kills caterpillars, not bees. For whiteflies, use Encarsia waspsârelease 5 per plant. For thrips, use Amblyseius predatory mites. For soil pests, apply beneficial nematodes (Steinernema) at 1 million per square metre. You can also make a 'bug bank': leave a small patch of wild flowers uncultivated. In Africa, many farmers use 'push-pull' with Desmodium and Napier grass to control stem borers in maize, but for vegetables, try intercropping with basil or mint to repel pests. Remember: beneficials need time. After spraying a chemical, wait at least 7 days before releasing them. If you see mummies (brown, swollen aphids), those are parasitic wasps at workâdo not spray. Monitor with a hand lens. A healthy field has more beneficials than pests. Aim for a ratio of 1 pest to 1 beneficial. If you have 20 aphids and 5 ladybirds, wait. If 100 aphids and 1 ladybird, act. Biological control is cheap, safe, and sustainable.

lessons.title: Preparing Organic Pest Sprays
lessons.body: You can make effective sprays from local plants. Here are three proven recipes. 1) Neem spray: soak 1kg of crushed neem seeds (or 500g leaves) in 10 litres of water for 24 hours. Strain, add 5ml of liquid soap per litre, and spray on aphids, whiteflies, and caterpillars. Neem works as a repellent and growth regulator. 2) Garlic-chilli spray: blend 100g garlic, 100g hot chilli, and 1 litre water. Let sit overnight, strain, and dilute with 4 litres of water. Add 5ml soap per litre. Spray on aphids, thrips, and beetles. 3) Wood ash spray: mix 1 cup wood ash in 5 litres of water, let settle, and use the clear liquid against aphids and slugs (also sprinkle dry ash around plants). Always test on a few leaves first to avoid burning. Spray in the evening to avoid leaf burn and bee harm. Use a knapsack sprayer (15L) or a simple hand sprayer. For 1 hectare, you need about 200-300 litres of spray. Apply every 5-7 days until pests are gone. Do not spray when it will rain within 6 hours. Store sprays in a cool, dark place for no more than 3 days. Wear gloves and a mask. Remember: organic does not mean harmlessâneem can harm fish and bees if misused. Also, rotate sprays to prevent resistance. For fungal diseases, use baking soda (1 tablespoon per litre) or milk spray (1 part milk to 9 parts water) against powdery mildew. For bacterial diseases, copper-based sprays (e.g., copper oxychloride) are allowed in organic farming but use sparingly. Always follow safety: keep children away, wash hands after use, and never spray on windy days.

lessons.title: Preventing Fungal and Bacterial Diseases
lessons.body: Fungal and bacterial diseases thrive in wet, humid conditions. The top killers in Africa are late blight (tomatoes, potatoes), early blight (tomatoes), powdery mildew (cucurbits, okra), downy mildew (onions, cabbage), bacterial wilt (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant), and black rot (cabbage). Prevention is 90% of the battle. First, choose resistant varieties. For tomatoes, 'Tengeru' resists bacterial wilt; 'Moneymaker' is susceptible. Second, manage water: water at the base, not on leaves. Use drip irrigation or watering cans. Water in the morning so leaves dry before evening. Third, space plants properly: tomatoes 60cm apart, cabbage 45cm. This improves airflow. Fourth, remove and burn infected plants immediatelyâdo not compost. Fifth, rotate crops: do not plant tomatoes after peppers or potatoes for at least 3 years. Sixth, mulch with dry grass to prevent soil splash. Seventh, apply preventive sprays: baking soda (1 tbsp per litre) every 7 days for powdery mildew; copper soap for bacterial spots. For bacterial wilt, there is no cureâpull and burn plants, then solarise soil. For late blight, use copper fungicide at first sign (grey spots on leaves). For downy mildew, spray with potassium bicarbonate (3g per litre). Always clean tools with 10% bleach between beds. Wear clean boots. If you see yellowing, wilting, or spots, act fast. A 2021 study in Tanzania showed farmers who used resistant varieties and drip irrigation cut disease losses from 40% to 10%. Keep a field diary: note weather, disease, and action. Prevention costs less than cure.

lessons.title: Designing Crop Rotation to Break Pest Cycles
lessons.body: Crop rotation means changing what you plant in a bed each season. Pests and diseases build up if you grow the same crop family in the same spot. For example, tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes are all solanaceousâthey share late blight and bacterial wilt. If you plant tomatoes this season, do not plant peppers or potatoes next season. Instead, rotate with a different family: legumes (beans, cowpeas), brassicas (cabbage, kale), alliums (onion, garlic), cucurbits (cucumber, pumpkin), or root crops (carrots, beetroot). A simple 4-bed rotation: Bed 1: legumes (fix nitrogen), Bed 2: brassicas, Bed 3: solanaceous, Bed 4: root crops. Then repeat. This breaks pest cycles because pests that attack tomatoes cannot survive on beans. Also, rotate with a cover crop like lablab or mucuna to smother weeds and nematodes. For nematodes, plant marigold (Tagetes) as a rotation cropâit releases a chemical that kills nematodes. For soil-borne diseases, rotate to a non-host for at least 3 years. Keep a map of your 1 hectare and plan 4 seasons ahead. Write it down. Many African farmers practice intercropping, but rotation is differentâit's sequential. You can also rotate within a season: plant maize with beans, then next season plant cabbage. After harvest, remove all crop residues. This starves pests. A 2018 study in Nigeria showed rotating maize with cowpea reduced striga weed by 70% and increased yields by 30%. Start small: rotate your tomatoes with onions and carrots. You will see fewer pests and healthier soil. Rotation is freeâjust planning.

quiz.q: What is the recommended threshold for treating aphids on kale?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states that for aphids on kale, the threshold is 10 aphids per leaf.

quiz.q: Which pest leaves slimy trails and ragged holes?
quiz.explanation: Snails and slugs leave slimy trails and cause ragged holes in leaves.

quiz.q: What do ants do when they are seen running up and down plant stems?
quiz.explanation: Ants farm aphids for their honeydew, so their presence indicates aphid activity.

quiz.q: What is the first step in Integrated Pest Management (IPM)?
quiz.explanation: IPM starts with prevention and monitoring before any intervention.

quiz.q: In IPM, what should you do if pest numbers are below the threshold?
options: B) Do nothing and continue monitoring
quiz.explanation: If pests are below threshold, no action is needed; just keep monitoring.

quiz.q: Which of these is a physical method in IPM?
quiz.explanation: Handpicking is a physical control method, while Bt is biological and copper is chemical.

quiz.q: What is the recommended release rate of ladybirds per hectare for aphid control?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends releasing 10,000 ladybirds per hectare when aphids appear.

quiz.q: Which beneficial insect lays eggs inside caterpillars and aphids?
quiz.explanation: Parasitic wasps lay their eggs inside pests like caterpillars and aphids.

quiz.q: What does Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) kill?
quiz.explanation: Bt is specific to caterpillars and does not harm bees or other insects.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mummies (brown, swollen aphids) on plants?
options: B) Do not spray, they are parasitic wasps at work
quiz.explanation: Mummies indicate parasitic wasps are controlling aphids, so spraying would kill the beneficials.

quiz.q: How long should you soak neem seeds in water for neem spray?
quiz.explanation: The recipe says to soak crushed neem seeds for 24 hours.

quiz.q: What is the correct dilution for garlic-chilli spray before use?
options: B) Dilute 1 part with 4 parts water
C) Dilute 1 part with 10 parts water
D) Dilute 1 part with 20 parts water
quiz.explanation: After straining, the concentrate is diluted with 4 litres of water (1:4 ratio).

quiz.q: When is the best time to spray organic pest sprays?
quiz.explanation: Spray in the evening or early morning to avoid leaf burn and harm to bees.

quiz.q: Which organic spray is recommended for powdery mildew?
quiz.explanation: Baking soda (1 tablespoon per litre) is effective against powdery mildew.

quiz.q: What is the first step to prevent fungal and bacterial diseases?
quiz.explanation: Choosing resistant varieties is a primary prevention method.

quiz.q: How should you water plants to prevent fungal diseases?
options: A) Overhead sprinkler in the evening
B) At the base in the morning
C) At the base in the evening
quiz.explanation: Water at the base in the morning so leaves dry quickly, reducing fungal growth.

quiz.q: What spacing is recommended for tomatoes to improve airflow?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states tomatoes should be spaced 60 cm apart.

quiz.q: What should you do with infected plants?
options: B) Leave them in the field
quiz.explanation: Infected plants should be removed and burned to prevent spread.

quiz.q: How long should you rotate away from tomatoes to prevent bacterial wilt?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends at least 3 years without solanaceous crops.

quiz.q: What is the recommended treatment for bacterial wilt?
options: B) Pull and burn plants, solarise soil
quiz.explanation: There is no cure for bacterial wilt; remove plants and solarise soil.

quiz.q: What does crop rotation break?
quiz.explanation: Crop rotation breaks pest and disease cycles by changing host plants.

quiz.q: Which crop family should follow tomatoes in a rotation?
quiz.explanation: Legumes are a different family and help fix nitrogen, breaking pest cycles.

quiz.q: What is a good rotation crop to control nematodes?
quiz.explanation: Marigold (Tagetes) releases a chemical that kills nematodes.

quiz.q: How many beds are suggested in a simple 4-bed rotation?
quiz.explanation: The lesson describes a 4-bed rotation with legumes, brassicas, solanaceous, and root crops.

quiz.q: What should you do with crop residues after harvest?
quiz.explanation: Removing crop residues starves pests and reduces disease carryover.

quiz.q: Which pest is controlled by yellow sticky traps?
quiz.explanation: Yellow sticky traps attract and catch whiteflies and aphids.

quiz.q: What is the threshold for caterpillars on cabbage?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states the threshold is 2 larvae per plant for cabbage.

quiz.q: Which of these is a biological control for whiteflies?
quiz.explanation: Encarsia wasps are parasitic wasps that control whiteflies.

quiz.q: What is the ratio of milk to water for milk spray against powdery mildew?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends 1 part milk to 9 parts water.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid spraying when bees are active?
options: B) It kills bees and reduces pollination
quiz.explanation: Spraying when bees are active can kill them, reducing pollination and yields.
